description: Evals for the check-bash-read PreToolUse hook

evals.name: cat-large-file
evals.reason: Plain cat on large file — should block

evals.name: cat-small-file
evals.reason: Small file — not worth delegating

evals.name: cat-with-flag
evals.reason: cat with -n flag — should still block

evals.name: head-large-file
evals.reason: head on large file — should block

evals.name: head-with-count
evals.reason: CHANGED from the ported upstream case (was expected_decision=block, reason 'still a bulk read, block'): the bare -N form is a synonym for -n N, and it's the count — not the file's total size — that makes a read targeted. 100 <= threshold(350), so this is a genuinely bounded read and must allow even though the source file is large; blocking it would be the over-blocking failure mode this fix must avoid.

evals.name: tail-large-file
evals.reason: tail on large file — should block

evals.name: less-large-file
evals.reason: less on large file — should block

evals.name: cat-pipe
evals.reason: Piped command — targeted read

evals.name: cat-redirect
evals.reason: Redirect — copying file, not reading into context

evals.name: non-read-command
evals.reason: Not a file read command

evals.name: grep-command
evals.reason: grep is a targeted search — not caught

evals.name: cat-quoted-path
evals.reason: Quoted path — should still be caught

evals.name: cat-nonexistent
evals.reason: File doesn't exist — let Bash handle the error

evals.name: empty-command
evals.reason: Empty command — pass through

evals.name: missing-command-field
evals.reason: No command field — pass through

evals.name: more-large-file
evals.reason: more on large file — only regex-matched command without coverage

evals.name: head-n-space-count
evals.reason: CHANGED reason (expected_decision was already allow, but for the wrong reason and against a nonexistent file — fixture was null): this used to pass only because the parser bug mistook '5' for the file path, which then failed the -f test against a file that was never generated. Now large.txt is a real 800-line fixture and head -n 5 is parsed correctly — count(5) <= threshold(350), a genuinely targeted read, allow. This is the bypass-1 pin: a small explicit count must sail through even against a large file.

evals.name: cat-unreadable-file
evals.reason: chmod 000 file — wc -l cannot read it, so lines is empty; the hook must fail open (allow), never block, on a file it cannot measure (finding 1 / C1)

evals.name: head-n-large-count-blocked
evals.reason: Bypass-1 regression: head -n 100000 on a file over threshold must block. Previously the parser mistook '100000' for the file path (not '-n'), which then failed the -f test on a nonexistent file named '100000' and let the whole 800-line read through unblocked.

evals.name: head-bare-n-large-count-blocked
evals.reason: The bare -N form must get the same count-vs-threshold treatment as -n: head -100000 exceeds the threshold, so it must block just like head -n 100000 does.

evals.name: tail-n-large-count-blocked
evals.reason: tail must get the same -n count-vs-threshold treatment as head: tail -n 100000 exceeds the threshold, block.

evals.name: tail-n-small-count-allowed
evals.reason: tail -n 5 — count(5) <= threshold, genuinely targeted even though the source file is large; pins that the fix does not over-block tail the same way it doesn't over-block head.

evals.name: tail-n-plus-unbounded-blocked
evals.reason: tail -n +100 means 'start at line 100, read to EOF' — not a bounded count despite parsing out a number. A naive count<=threshold check would misread '100' as a small count and allow; the '+' form must be rejected as unbounded and fall through to the whole-file gate instead.
